name: Nikhil Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics in Edinburgh. Mornings I'm at the boat club at six for rowing, then lectures, then the library, and evenings I cook with my flatmates Callum and Priya. On Saturdays I do a few hours of stats practice, because maths is the part I enjoy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why economics, and how are your parents involved?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum is a branch manager at a bank and my dad's a surveyor, so I grew up with money and buildings as the dinner table topics. They pay my fees and rent, and I've no debt. I like economics because it lets you ask boring questions about real things, like why a shop closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it matches what I thought: a handy tool, useful for spreadsheets, but not a game changer. I'd tell the boat club that the economy is still about wages, housing and interest rates. I wouldn't spend time arguing online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. Banks have used software for decades, so another layer doesn't scare me. Entry-level analyst jobs might get a bit less routine, but I'd expect to get one around 2030 without much trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: rowing, lectures, and a summer internship at a bank or a consultancy. I'd use the AI helper for coding and spreadsheets now and then, since it saves time. I'd also keep up my stats practice, because quantitative skills are the safe bet either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to fight about. It feels like the normal worries of a first year, such as which modules to take and whether I'll get an internship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who is worried about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend worried about AI? That the loud predictions have been wrong before, and that learning a skill like statistics is safe in most worlds. I'd also say don't switch courses over a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually use the tool for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you actually use the tool for? Checking my R code when it won't run, and explaining a concept in a different way. I don't paste in essays, because I'd rather do the thinking myself and it's often wrong in subtle ways. Statistics is a safe skill in most worlds, so I'd tell a worried friend not to switch courses over a headline.

say: I'd say it's **a handy tool**, not a game changer.
I'd tell the boat club it's still **wages, housing and rates**.
think: Banks have used software for decades, so another layer **doesn't scare me**.
I'd expect a **graduate role** around 2030 without much trouble.
do: Keep rowing, lectures and stats practice, and apply for a **summer internship**.
Use the AI helper for **code and spreadsheets** now and then.
feel: **Calm**: only the normal first-year worries about modules and internships.
S0.quote: Statistics is a safe skill in most worlds, so I'd tell a worried friend not to switch courses over a headline.
fieldNote: Nikhil's calm is **well-founded**: strong cushion, quantitative skills and a mild scenario.
He uses AI in a narrow way and gives a clear reason for not pasting in essays.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a bank or consultancy
Keep up weekly statistics practice on Saturdays
Use the AI helper to check my R code and spreadsheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds plausible, and that it's the sort of change economists have studied before, such as spreadsheets and the internet. I'd tell friends the tasks shift and the jobs shift more slowly. I'd say wait and see what firms actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think some of the junior analyst work shrinks, such as reports, data pulls and summaries. But the people who can oversee it and explain results will be valued. I'd expect a smaller number of graduate roles, but I'd be competitive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into the skills that sit above the routine. I'd take modules in econometrics and finance, and learn the tools better, since they're proven now. I'd apply for placements early, and I'd ask my mum what her bank is cutting and what it's hiring for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some focus. I'd feel a bit more pressure to stand out, but I like clear goals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum, the bank manager, tell you she's seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What did your mum say when you asked? In this picture, she'd say the back office and call centre shrink first, while relationship roles stay. That's useful, because it tells me to learn to deal with clients and not only numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you wrong about being fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you wrong about being fine? If every bank cut graduate hiring in half at once. I'd have to rethink and maybe aim at a different industry, like public bodies or property. The back office shrinks first and client-facing roles stay, so I'd learn to deal with clients as well as numbers.

say: I'd say it's **plausible** and like past shifts, with tasks changing before jobs.
I'd tell friends to **wait and see** what firms actually do.
think: Junior analyst work shrinks, but people who can **oversee and explain** results stay valued.
I'd expect **fewer graduate roles**, but I'd be competitive.
do: Take **econometrics and finance** modules and learn the tools properly.
Ask my mum what her **bank cuts and hires**.
feel: **Calm** with some focus, a little more pressure to stand out.
S1.quote: The back office shrinks first and client-facing roles stay, so I'd learn to deal with clients as well as numbers.
fieldNote: Nikhil is **calm** because he sees tasks shifting rather than careers ending, and has a skill plan.
His honest limit: if every bank halved graduate hiring, he would have to change industry.

steps.text: Learn AI tools properly now that they are proven
Ask my mum which bank roles are shrinking and which are hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a real emergency and that governments should prepare now. I'd ask my economics lecturers what the models say, and say publicly that the speed is the problem, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. My degree ends in 2029, after AGI, and economics jobs are thinking jobs. The finance sector is full of them. I'd expect hiring to freeze, and I might be one of a lot of graduates with nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents and ask if their jobs are safe, since my mum's bank would change fast. I'd stay on the degree but treat it as general training, and I'd look at the physical side of the economy, like property and infrastructure, which my dad knows. I'd keep money in simple accounts rather than shares, and I'd learn the tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the speed that gets me. My plan has a whole structure around it that wouldn't hold up in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is two years different from the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How is two years different from the slower versions? It's the difference between adapting and improvising. With ten years I'd redo my plan. With two I'd be making decisions based on a few headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign you'd watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would be the first sign you'd watch for? Whether my mum's bank stops hiring graduates and starts offering early retirement. That would tell me more than any news story. With ten years I'd redo my plan, but with two years I'd be making decisions based on a few headlines.

say: I'd say it's **a real emergency** and governments should prepare now.
I'd say the **speed** is the problem, not the technology.
think: My degree ends in **2029**, after AGI, and finance is full of thinking jobs.
I might be one of **many graduates** with nowhere to go.
do: Treat the degree as **general training** and look at property and infrastructure.
Keep money in **simple accounts** and learn the tools properly.
feel: **Anxious**: the plan has a structure that wouldn't hold in two years.
S2.quote: With ten years I'd redo my plan, but with two years I'd be making decisions based on a few headlines.
fieldNote: Nikhil's anxiety is about **speed**, because his steady style needs time to test things.
He picks a concrete signal to watch: graduate hiring at his mother's bank.

steps.text: Move spare money into simple savings accounts rather than shares
Ask my parents how safe their bank and surveying jobs are
Learn the AI tools properly during second year
Watch whether my mum's bank stops hiring graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and that planning should start now. I'd tell friends to keep studying but not to bet on one narrow job. I'd also raise it at the economics society as a debate topic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel uneasy, but not scared. I'd have two years of work before 2031, and my parents' cushion would cover the gaps. The thing I'd fear is that everyone in my field has the same idea at the same time and that wipes out the advantage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and look for a role that sits close to physical assets, where robots arrive later, like property finance. I'd learn the tools properly and build some small data projects. I'd save as much as I can in the first job and keep my costs low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a pressure rather than a panic, like an exam date that's circled in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is five years giving you that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What is five years giving you that two didn't? Time to test. I could try one career for a year, see what's changing, and still switch. That's how I like to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents? That they should plan their own retirement conservatively. Mum's bank could change a lot by 2031, and I'd want her pension and savings simple. Five years lets me test one career for a year, see what is changing, and still switch.

say: I'd say five years is **short but workable** and planning should start now.
I'd tell friends not to bet on **one narrow job**.
think: I'd have two years of work before 2031 and my parents' **cushion** behind me.
I fear everyone has the **same idea** at once.
do: Look for roles near **physical assets**, like property finance, and build data projects.
**Save hard** in the first job and keep costs low.
feel: **Uneasy**: a pressure, like an exam date circled in the diary.
S3.quote: Five years lets me test one career for a year, see what is changing, and still switch.
fieldNote: Nikhil's **steady** style shows: he wants to test one career for a year before committing.
He also looks after his parents' plans, treating the bank job as at risk.

steps.text: Aim for a first job in property finance, where robots arrive later
Build small data projects to show my skills
Save hard and keep costs low in the first job
Suggest my parents keep their pensions and savings simple

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to adapt if people use it sensibly. I'd tell friends to keep learning and not panic. I wouldn't change anything dramatic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd be 28, and I could have worked in three different roles. If things change, I'd have savings and experience, and I'd adapt as the evidence comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work a couple of years, and maybe do a master's in data or finance if it still makes sense. I'd keep rowing and keep my life balanced. I'd also save steadily, because savings are the most flexible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off, and I trust myself to adjust when something becomes clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could ten years make you complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Does ten years make you complacent? It could. I'd set a check each year: what has changed in jobs, what are people hiring for, and does my plan still fit. A diary note is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier than planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you move earlier than planned? If a respected firm or a government report said the date was getting closer. I'd move once, then, with good information. I'd rather wait for the evidence and move once, than jump at every headline and have to move twice.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough to adapt** if people use it sensibly.
I'd tell friends to keep learning and **not panic**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and could have had **three roles**.
I'd have **savings and experience** and adapt as evidence comes.
do: Finish the degree, work **two years**, then decide about a master's.
Save steadily and make an **annual check** of my plan.
feel: **Calm**: far off, and he trusts himself to adjust when things become clear.
S4.quote: I'd rather wait for the evidence and move once, than jump at every headline and have to move twice.
fieldNote: Nikhil's calm comes with **a habit**: a yearly review so that ten years doesn't breed complacency.
He would move earlier only on good evidence from respected sources.

steps.text: Finish the degree and work two years before deciding on more study
Review my plan each year in a diary note
Consider a master's in data or finance if it still fits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because banks, rules and families all move slowly, and it would catch every one of them unprepared. What would help is clear, fast guidance from governments and a safety net that's already built, so households aren't improvising.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really, except that I tend to wait for evidence and I know that can look like caution. I'd say I'm steady, not slow, and I think that matters more when things are unclear. I would rather be steady than slow, and steady matters more when nobody is sure what happens next.

headlineQuote: I would rather be steady than slow, and steady matters more when nobody is sure what happens next.
portrait: **Nikhil** is an 18-year-old economics student in Edinburgh, whose parents, a bank manager and a surveyor, pay everything.
He is **pragmatic and centrist**, and uses AI now and then for spreadsheets and code, after others have tried it.
He judges change by **evidence**: calm when it is slow or hype, tense when it is fast.
In the milder worlds he expects to **adapt** into oversight and analysis roles, and mood moves with the warning time.
He relies on his **parents' bank and property** knowledge to ground his plans.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, because banks, rules and families would all be caught unprepared.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **fast clear guidance** from governments and a safety net built beforehand.
